column4: It gives the section's distinction in an explicit command: do not prostrate to the sun or moon; prostrate to Allah who created them, matching the move from celestial lights to إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ.

Before Abraham's observations of the setting lights, this ayah says he was shown the dominion of the heavens and earth; it supplies the cosmic frame in which the following star, moon, and sun are judged as creatures.

Abraham sees a star and calls it his lord only within the test of its setting; “those that set” cannot be loved as lord. It begins the section's contrast between a visible heavenly light and the true Lord.

The moon rises and then sets; Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would belong to the astray people. This directly joins the lunar scene to the source's Rab, hidayah, and dallin language.
The sun rises, is called the larger heavenly body, then sets; Abraham disavows association. It is the source's fullest solar reversal of treating a rising light as divine.
Abraham turns his face toward the Originator of the heavens and earth as a hanif. It supplies the positive direction after the star, moon, and sun have proved unfit as objects of devotion.
Abraham's Lord has guided him to a straight, upright religion. It connects the source's Ibrahim scene to the mustaqim/Q-W-M family without making the noon sense into a further doctrine.
This ayah identifies the ruler as a woman governing the people. Its own contribution is the particular detail that the source places immediately before the report of that people's solar worship.
The hoopoe finds her people prostrating to the sun apart from Allah, and says they have been turned from the path and are not guided. It directly binds solar worship to the loss of the way.

Continuing the same report, it says prostration belongs to Allah, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and earth. It states the Creator-directed alternative to the people's prostration to the sun.
Allah makes the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and apportions the moon's stations for years and reckoning. This is the section's moon-mansion and measured-time image in Qur'anic form.
The new crescents are appointed measures of time for people and pilgrimage. It directly gives the hilal its practical timekeeping role rather than a divine status.
The splitter of dawn makes night for rest and the sun and moon for calculation. It gathers daybreak, the daily rhythm, and celestial measurement into one created order.
Night is stripped from day and people are left in darkness. It makes the section's turning daily sky a visible transition rather than a static backdrop.
The sun runs toward its fixed course by the decree of the Mighty, Knowing. Its movement answers the image of the sun at midday and its later descent with a measured course.
The moon is assigned stations until it returns like an old date stalk. This gives a Qur'anic sequence behind the source's crescent and lunar-station details.
The sun does not overtake the moon, night does not outstrip day, and each swims in an orbit. It marks the ordered boundaries among the lights and times that the image holds together.
Allah creates night, day, sun, and moon, each swimming in an orbit. This is a compact account of the celestial sphere and its moving contents.
The sun and moon are by calculation. It reinforces the source's account of a measurable day and the moon's counted stations.
Allah raises the sky and sets the balance. It places the image's two linked expressions—an elevated sky and the day's balance becoming upright—side by side without collapsing their distinct meanings.
Allah extends the shadow and makes the sun its indicator. This directly clarifies the source's noon image by showing shadow's dependence on the sun.
The next ayah says the extended shadow is then withdrawn gradually. Its own contribution is the temporal change in shadow that gives the nearly shadowless zenith its place in a larger daily movement.

At sunrise the sun inclines away from the cave to the right, and at sunset passes them on the left; the ayah ends by naming Allah's guidance. It joins directional shadow to the source's straight way and hidayah.
The sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, and creatures prostrate to Allah. It reverses solar and lunar worship: the heavenly bodies belong among those bowing to their Creator.
Allah creates the heavens and earth, covers day with night in rapid pursuit, and makes sun, moon, and stars subject to His command. It supplies the daily sky as an ordered act of lordship.
Allah wraps night over day and day over night, and subjects sun and moon until an appointed term. It connects the image's daily alternation to the finitude and service of its lights.
Those questioned acknowledge that Allah created the heavens and earth and subjected sun and moon. The verse exposes the inconsistency of recognizing the Creator while directing devotion elsewhere.
Allah subjects night, day, sun, moon, and stars, calling them signs for people who understand. It treats the image's lights as intelligible signs under command.
The sun and moon are made constantly serviceable, as are night and day. It gives the daily cycle the character of provision rather than deity.
After raising the heavens, Allah subjects sun and moon, each running to a fixed term. It joins the overhead sky to the finite courses of its two most visible lights.
Allah merges night into day and day into night and subjects sun and moon for an appointed term. It describes the transition around the day the source defines from sunrise to sunset.
Allah inserts night into day and day into night, and subjects sun and moon, each moving to a fixed term. It makes the image's alternation and celestial timing acts of Allah.
Allah places constellations in the sky and makes there a lamp and a luminous moon. It presents the sky's visible lights as things He made and placed.
Allah makes the moon a light among the heavens and makes the sun a lamp. Its distinct functions sharpen the source's paired moon-and-sun image.
The oath by the sun and its brightness isolates the solar light that fills the section's daytime sky.
The moon follows the sun. It gives a concise relation between the two lights in the source's ordered sky.
Day discloses the sun. It directly stages the day as the sun-lit span described in the source.
Night covers the sun. Along with the preceding ayat, it makes the daily covering and uncovering of the light explicit.
Abraham answers the claimant of lordship by saying Allah brings the sun from the east and challenging him to bring it from the west. The solar horizon becomes evidence against a false lord.
Praise is directed to Allah in the evening, morning, late afternoon, and at noon. It gives the daily stations, including the source's noon, a worshipful response.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord before sunrise and before sunset. It brackets the source's day by its solar limits and directs speech to the Lord rather than the sun.
After commanding patience, the ayah commands praise before sunrise and before sunset. Its two solar edges frame devotion in the same daily span.
Prayer is set from the sun's decline until night darkness, with the dawn recitation. It maps worship across the changing solar day rather than toward the heavenly body.
Prayer is commanded at the two ends of the day and in approaches of the night. It divides the source's sun-bounded day into acts of worship.
If Allah made night continuous, no god other than Him could bring light. The rhetorical question denies a rival ilah the power over the celestial light that sun worship would assume.
If Allah made day continuous, no god other than Him could bring night for rest. It supplies the reciprocal boundary of the daily cycle and sole divine control of it.
Allah is Lord of east and west, with no deity but Him, so He is to be taken as guardian. The horizon-pair is explicitly joined to exclusive devotion.
The creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding. It states the reflective frame for the section's whole sky image.

The continuation declares that Allah alone is God and Lord of the magnificent throne. In the solar-worship passage, it completes the report's shift from the queen's people to the One they should worship.
The queen finally says she submits with Solomon to the Lord of the worlds. It is the narrative resolution of the woman's earlier solar worship, though the ayah itself no longer names the sun.
The shadows of all created things turn right and left in prostration to Allah. Their directional motion contrasts with the source's balanced noon shadow and turns that scene toward worship.
The shadows of those in the heavens and earth prostrate morning and evening. It gives the changing length and direction of shadow a cosmic posture toward Allah.
Among Allah's signs, heaven and earth stand by His command. Its standing language from the Q-W-M family makes a restrained cosmic parallel to the source's upright sun and balanced day.
Allah makes the sky a canopy over people. This is a direct Qur'anic instance of the source's dictionary sense of sama as what is above and gives cover.
Allah makes the sky a protected ceiling. It develops the image of the overhead sky as a made enclosure rather than an object of reverence.
People are asked to look at the sky above them—how Allah built and adorned it without fissures. It gives the visible vault in the source an explicitly created form.
Allah is named as Lord of Sirius. Naming a star's Lord makes a pointed celestial parallel to the source's refusal to treat a visible heavenly light as lord.
Allah makes stars so people can find their way through the darkness of land and sea. It distinguishes their created navigational guidance from the Lord's guidance sought by Abraham.
Landmarks and stars guide travelers. This gives a concrete celestial counterpart to the source's straight-path language without equating physical navigation with salvation.
“Worship Me; this is a straight path” states the positive relation that 27:24 reverses: devotion to something other than Allah turns people away from the path.

Jesus says Allah is his Lord and their Lord, then commands worship of Him as a straight path. This gives another explicit worship-and-straightness formulation relevant to the source's solar-worship contrast.
Jesus declares Allah his Lord and their Lord and says to worship Him; that is a straight path. It repeats the same concrete relation between exclusive worship and the path.
Jesus commands worship of Allah, his Lord and theirs, calling it a straight path. It clarifies the positive direction opposite the sun-worshippers' blocked path.
Allah calls His way straight and commands following it rather than divergent ways. It sharpens the path boundary that 27:24 says solar worship breaches.
Allah is Lord of the two easts and the two wests. The plural horizons give a celestial extension of the source's sunrise-to-sunset frame.
East and west belong to Allah, and wherever one turns is Allah's face. It resonates with Abraham's turning his face to the Creator rather than to a rising body on the horizon.
Allah is Lord of the heavens, earth, what lies between them, and the easts. It names the celestial totality and horizons as belonging to one Lord.
The oath invokes the Lord of the easts and wests. It makes the recurring horizons of the daily sun an aspect of divine lordship.
Allah makes night and day two signs so people may seek bounty and know the count of years and reckoning. It supplies a day-and-night counterpart to the moon's measured calendar.
The alternation of night and day and what Allah creates in the heavens and earth are signs for the mindful. It explicitly joins temporal alternation to the populated sky.
Allah makes night for rest and day for sight. It assigns the daily sky's two conditions human purposes, echoing the source's definition of day.
From mercy Allah makes night for rest and day for seeking bounty. It gives the day-and-night rhythm a provided function rather than independent power.
Allah darkens the heaven's night and brings out its brightness. It renders the source's day/night sky as a deliberate alternation in the heaven itself.
The oath by the bright morning gives the dawn-side of the solar day a distinct visual presence.
The still night completes the preceding morning scene with the other side of the daily rhythm.
The verse names the time when people put aside clothes at noon, between dawn and night privacy times. It is a direct human-time marker for the source's midday moment.
Allah makes shades from what He has created and shelters in the mountains. It gives a concrete beneficent instance of the source's secondary sama sense: what is above can give shade.
Allah shades the Children of Israel with clouds. The overhead cloud makes the source's “what rises above and shades” definition tangible.
In the division of Israel into tribes, Allah shades them with the cloud. This repeats the overhanging sheltering scene in a distinct passage.
Addressing Israel, Allah recalls shading them with clouds. It preserves the same provided overhead cover within a direct divine address.
The mountain is raised over Israel like a canopy as they fear it falling. It is a threatening reversal of the source's sky-as-overhead-cover image.
Allah places constellations in the sky and beautifies it for observers. It fills the source's sky sphere with visible created markers, including the kind of star Abraham sees.
Allah adorns the lowest heaven with the adornment of stars. It presents the stellar sky as an adornment made by its Lord.
Allah adorns the nearest heaven with lamps and assigns it protection. It provides a created-heaven setting for lights that humans must not worship.
Allah adorns the nearest heaven with lamps. The ayah's own depiction of stars as placed lamps supports the source's creature-versus-Creator distinction.
The Prophet is told to remember his Lord's name morning and evening. It gives the day’s opening and closing light a response parallel to the source's exclusive worship.
The oath by the moon when it becomes full is the lunar boundary opposite the source's newly risen crescent; together they make the moon's changing form perceptible.
In Joseph's dream, the sun, moon, and eleven stars are the ones prostrating. As a dream image, it reverses the direction of solar and lunar prostration in the source's worship contrast.
Shade and scorching heat are declared unequal. This sharpens the source's nearly absent noon shadow by setting shade against the sun's burning opposite.
At the final upheaval the moon is darkened. The loss of its light is a boundary against treating the changing moon of the source as divine.
The sun and moon are brought together at the final upheaval. Their ordinary ordered separation in the source's sky is reversed, showing both are subject to a greater command.
The sun is folded up at the final upheaval. The reversal of its daily shining underscores that the solar light is a created, ending sign.
The stars lose their light or fall away at the final upheaval. Against Abraham's setting star, this is the cosmic limit of the same visible lights.
People are sent to a three-branched “shade” in the fire scene. It is a severe reversal of the source's overhead shade, since the following ayah denies it gives real shelter.
The following ayah says that this shade is neither cool nor protective from flame. Its own contribution fixes the contrast with a true overhead shade.

After the celestial argument, Abraham says that Allah has guided him and that he does not fear the things his people associate with Him. Its own contribution is the passage's explicit contrast between guidance and feared false associates.

Abraham asks why he should fear their associates when they do not fear associating with Allah without authority. It carries the preceding sun-and-moon rejection into a direct argument against association.

The conclusion of Abraham's exchange gives security and guidance to those whose faith is not mixed with wrongdoing. It supplies the passage's answer to the source's danger of becoming among the astray.
Allah makes night and day succeed one another for whoever wishes to remember or give thanks. It turns the source's revolving daily sky into a sequence calling for response to Allah.
The command is to prostrate and glorify Allah during the night and at the retreat of the stars. It pairs a setting-star scene with worship directed away from the star.

Immediately after the oath by the descending star, the ayah says the Messenger has neither gone astray nor erred. Its own contribution directly joins the star scene to the source's hidayah-and-dalal contrast.
Continuing the moving-shadow image, creatures in the heavens and earth and the angels prostrate to Allah. It widens 16:48's visual prostration into an explicit cosmic worship scene.
Dhu al-Qarnayn reaches the place of sunset and sees the sun setting at a spring. It gives the source's sunset boundary a concrete horizon scene, while remaining a traveler's observation.
At the place of sunrise, Dhu al-Qarnayn finds a people for whom Allah has made no shelter from it. The exposed rising sun reverses the source's secondary image of what is overhead giving shade.
Allah holds the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission. It makes the overhead heaven dependent on the Creator rather than an independent power.
Allah makes the sky a built structure and identifies Himself as Lord. It gives another concrete Qur'anic form to the source's overhead sama.
Allah builds seven strong layers above people. Its own contribution is the sky's deliberate overhead construction, which frames the following blazing light.
Allah raises the heaven's height and proportions it. It supplies the constructed vault whose night and brightness the next ayah describes.
The oath by the sky and the One who built it completes the surrounding sun, moon, day, and night scenes by naming their overhead setting as made.
Allah makes night for rest and day for seeing. It gives the day/night sky distinct human functions alongside the source's measured lights.
Allah makes night for rest and day for sight. Its repeated formulation presents the visible day as a divine favor, not an autonomous light.
Allah makes night a covering, sleep a rest, and day for waking activity. It adds a human rhythm to the source's passage from celestial light to darkness.
Allah alternates night and day, calling this a lesson for people of sight. The ayah explicitly makes the visual change in the sky an occasion for perception.
The alternation of night and day is listed among signs for people who understand. It connects the source's daily sequence to discernment in a passage that also looks to what comes from the sky.
Allah causes night to enter day and day to enter night while holding dominion. It supplies another direct formulation of the daily transition as sovereign action.
Allah causes night to enter day and day to enter night. Its own contribution is to ground that visible alternation in the hearing and seeing Lord.
Allah causes night to enter day and day to enter night, while knowing what is within hearts. It repeats the source's turning day-and-night image with an inward accountability dimension.

The rhetorical question asks who guides people through the darknesses of land and sea and whether there is any deity with Allah. It is a nonstellar parallel to the source's created celestial guidance and exclusive lordship.
The oath by night as it covers repeats the source's visual movement of darkness over the lit sky.
The oath by day as it shines gives the complementary emergence of visible daylight.
The oath is by the star when it descends. It closely resembles Abraham's setting-star scene; whether this descent is specifically a setting is interpretively uncertain.
The “blazing lamp” is commonly understood as the sun; on that reading, this ayah gives the source's midday light an intense created form. The solar referent is not named in the ayah itself.
The ayah says that a day with Allah is like a thousand years of human counting. It marks a deliberate boundary to the source's lexical daylight sense of yawm.
Allah directs the affair from heaven to earth, then it rises to Him in a day measured as a thousand human years. It combines the source's sky with a non-solar scale of yawm.
The angels and Spirit ascend to Allah in a day measured as fifty thousand years. This makes the source's day-word extend beyond the sunrise-to-sunset image into an explicitly different scale.
The stars are scattered at the final upheaval. It gives a further boundary to the ordinary, navigable stellar sky developed in the source.
